1.goal: To open the cycle on the situation it is about: a group deciding things in a chat, with her in it.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask when she last opened a group chat with forty messages and had to work out what had been decided. One answer, then move.
Say in one sentence what is different about this material: ten screens, a real situation, and her speaking is the product.
1.expected: One concrete example, almost certainly from school this week.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask about a family group or a sports team instead.
1.challenge: Ask what she did about it: did she scroll back, ask someone, or wait?
1.monitoring: Whether she describes reading as the problem or answering as the problem. It is the second.
1.evidence: The example she gives, and that she heard what this cycle is for.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example.

2.goal: To establish who the four people are, what the group owes, and that she is being asked for an opinion.
run: Give her time to read the card. Then confirm two things out loud: one work for the whole group, and the slides are due Sunday.
Do not explain the chat yet. The card is the situation, not the text.
2.expected: Immediate recognition. She does group work every week.
2.support: If she asks who Professor Okafor is, say only that she runs the seminar.
2.challenge: Ask what usually goes wrong in a group of four when nobody is in charge.
2.monitoring: Whether she sees the group as a task or as people. Both are fine; it tells you how she will speak in stage 7.
2.evidence: Her one-sentence version of what the group has to decide.
2.transition: Move on when she says, in one sentence, what has to be decided.

3.goal: To activate what she already knows about group chats before she reads this one.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions, no right answers.
run: Read the three questions with her and ask for a guess on each.
Do not correct anything here. These are hypotheses, and two of them will be tested by the chat.
3.expected: She has plenty to say. Let her talk.
3.support: If she answers in Portuguese, take the idea and give it back in English for her to repeat.
3.challenge: Ask which is worse in a chat: missing a date, or missing that someone is annoyed.
3.monitoring: Whether she already knows that silence can be agreement. If she does, the detail stage will be fast.
3.evidence: Her prediction about who ends up doing the unclaimed job.
3.transition: Move on when she has answered all three.

4.goal: One fast read of the whole chat, for the decision and the dates only.
4.interaction: S alone for 60 seconds, then T–S.
run: Sixty seconds of silent reading. Then the two questions on the screen, out loud.
Do not let this become a vocabulary lesson. If she asks about not it, answer in five words and move on.
4.expected: She reads it easily. The answers may still be vague about the second date.
4.support: If she hesitates, ask only: what is due, and when?
4.challenge: Ask her to say the whole chat in two sentences, as if she were texting someone else.
4.monitoring: Whether she separates the two dates, or collapses them into one.
4.evidence: Her first summary, before any analysis. Write down how many sentences it took.
4.transition: Move on when she has named the work and at least one date.

5.goal: To separate what the group decided from what somebody only suggested, and from what is not there.
5.interaction: S classifies, T checks. Discuss only the ones she gets wrong.
run: She classifies the six lines, then you check them together.
The item that decides this stage is the email to the professor: nobody took it. If she marks it as decided, name that out loud.
The Friday request was refused. A request that was answered no is not a decision, and it is the second most common mistake here.
5.expected: Answer key, item by item: The group is presenting the Vermeer -- the group decided it. The slides are due on Sunday -- the group decided it. The check-in call will move to Friday -- somebody suggested it, and Priya refused it in the next line. Somebody is emailing Professor Okafor -- it is not in the chat, both said not it. Priya has done the slides late before -- somebody suggested it, implied by the 2am line. Stella is presenting first -- it is not in the chat, nobody mentions the order. Expect four or five right on the first pass: the email and the Friday request are the two that separate a good reader from a fast one.
5.support: If she is unsure, ask: did anybody answer this line? What did they answer?
5.challenge: Ask her which of the six would still be unclear to somebody joining the group tomorrow.
5.monitoring: Whether she treats silence as agreement, and whether she notices Priya’s 2am line.
5.evidence: Which items she got wrong, and what she said when you asked why.
5.transition: Move on when all six are checked.

6.goal: That SHE formulates the difference between reacting to a chat and moving it forward. Do not hand her the rule.
6.interaction: S marks two of four, then T asks what they have in common.
run: Four replies on the screen. She marks the two that would move the group forward.
Then ask: what do the two you marked have in common?
The answer you want, in her words: they name something the group has not settled, and they give everyone something to correct.
6.expected: Answer key: Yeah, the Vermeer works for me, it’s a great painting -- no, it agrees and adds nothing. So what we’ve decided is the Vermeer, slides Sunday, call Thursday 6pm. Is that right? -- yes, it says the decision and both dates back. lol not it either -- no, a third refusal leaves the email where it was. One thing nobody has picked up is the email. I can take it if someone starts the slides -- yes, it names the job and puts a condition on taking it. She will probably get the two right and struggle to say why. The saying why is the stage.
6.support: If she cannot formulate it, ask what the other two leave the group to do next.
6.challenge: Ask her to write the third message the group needs, the one nobody has sent.
6.monitoring: Whether she can state a principle in her own words, without borrowing yours.
6.evidence: Her formulation, in her words, however rough.
6.transition: Move on when she has formulated the difference herself.

7.goal: The six openings said out loud, with content coming from you.
7.interaction: T gives raw content, S returns it with the opening. Six times, fast.
run: You say the content plainly (“they picked the Vermeer”, “nobody is emailing the professor”) and she gives it back using the opening on the screen.
Correct immediately here, and briefly. This is the form stage; in stage 7 you stop correcting.
If she stretches the sentence, ask for the same idea in half the words.
7.expected: The six come out at least once each. Two or three will still be clumsy.
7.support: If an opening does not come, give her the first three words and let her finish.
7.challenge: Take the openings off the screen and do three more from memory.
7.monitoring: Which openings she avoids. Those are the ones to give her in stage 7.
7.evidence: The two that came out most naturally, and the two she avoided.
7.transition: Move on when all six have been said at least once.

8.goal: Two minutes telling somebody who was not in the chat what was decided, what is open and what she is taking, with the chat closed.
8.interaction: S speaks, T is Tomas. One interruption, then silence.
run: CLOSE THE CHAT BEFORE SHE STARTS. With the text in sight she reads it out, and reading out is not what this lesson measures.
You are Tomas, who muted the group. Two minutes. Interrupt ONCE, in the middle, with “wait, who is emailing her?” and then let her find her way back.
THIS IS THE LESSON: the turn is hers. After you ask, WAIT. Her silence is work.
Do not correct during. Write it down, including register, and give it back in stage 8.
8.expected: Two minutes is longer than she expects. Expect one stall around the halfway mark, which is where your interruption helps.
8.support: If she stops early, ask one of the five bullets she has not covered.
8.challenge: Ask her to do it as a voice note she would actually send, with the same information.
8.monitoring: How many of the six openings she uses unprompted, whether she says both dates, and whether she names the unclaimed email.
8.evidence: Count of openings used, both dates said or not, the unclaimed job named or not, and one sentence that sounded like an essay rather than a person.
8.transition: Move on when she closes, or at two minutes, whichever comes first.

9.goal: To give back what you noticed and ask for the same thing in a third of the time.
9.interaction: T gives two points, S speaks again for 45 seconds.
run: Two things, no more: one that worked and one that did not come out. Direct and short.
Then: same thing, forty-five seconds, and Tomas is already walking into the classroom.
Do not add new content here. It is the same task under one changed constraint.
9.expected: The second version is usually clearer and more natural than the first.
9.support: If she freezes, give her the first opening and start the clock again.
9.challenge: Ask for it a third time in twenty seconds, keeping only what cannot be cut.
9.monitoring: What she CUTS. If the deadline or the unclaimed email goes, the hierarchy is not clear yet.
9.evidence: What she cut and what she kept, for the post-lesson record.
9.transition: Move on when the shorter version is done.
exact: Start her again with: So what we’ve decided is…

10.goal: To close on what she recognizes, and to point at where she will use it this week.
10.interaction: S marks the lists alone. T does not discuss the marks.
run: She marks what she recognizes. Do not argue with the marks: they are hers.
Homework, out loud and not on the screen: an optional 90-second recording about a real group she is in, plus two links.
Next lesson: ninety seconds of the group call, two people talking fast, and what to do at the exact point she loses the thread.
Fill in the post-lesson record before you close.
10.expected: She will mark the summarizing line high and the naming line lower.
10.support: If she marks everything at the top, ask which one she would still avoid in a real group.
10.challenge: Ask which of the six she would actually type today, and why that one.
10.monitoring: The gap between what she marks and what you observed in stage 7.
10.evidence: Her self-assessment, and your record, both written before the lesson ends.
